sortItems.text: Asking an AI tool to list possible topics related to your interest in marine biology.
sortItems.feedback: Brainstorming widens your options. You still choose, narrow, and research the topic.

sortItems.text: Asking an AI tool to write your persuasive speech and submitting it as your own.
sortItems.feedback: This replaces your thinking and misrepresents authorship. It is an academic integrity violation in most courses.

sortItems.text: Asking an AI tool to explain the difference between inductive and deductive reasoning with new examples.
sortItems.feedback: Using AI to understand a concept is like asking a tutor. Check the explanation against your textbook.

sortItems.text: Asking an AI tool to give you three statistics with sources for your speech, and using them without checking.
sortItems.feedback: AI tools can produce sources and numbers that do not exist. Every source must be found and read by you.

sortItems.text: Asking an AI tool to play a skeptical audience member and ask you tough questions about your argument.
sortItems.feedback: Practicing responses strengthens your reasoning, and the answers stay yours.

sortItems.text: Asking an AI tool to invent a personal story for your narrative speech.
sortItems.feedback: A personal narrative must be your experience. A fabricated story deceives your audience.

sortItems.text: Pasting your outline and asking which main point seems to need more evidence.
sortItems.feedback: Feedback on organization and gaps helps you revise your own work. Follow your teacher's rules about sharing work with AI tools.

sortItems.text: Copying an AI tool's analysis of a famous speech into your reflection without forming your own view.
sortItems.feedback: Analysis is the skill being learned. Use AI ideas only as something to agree or argue with, and say so.

stages.label: Finding a topic
questions: What have you experienced, studied, or done that most people your age haven't?
What problem in your school or community do you notice that others overlook?
Which of your ideas would your audience find new, useful, or surprising?
What do you already know about this, and what would you need to find out?

stages.label: Sharpening purpose and thesis
questions: In one sentence, what should your audience know, believe, or do when you finish?
Does your specific purpose contain the word "and"? If so, which half is the real speech?
If a friend asked "so what?" after hearing your central idea, what would you say?
Is your verb (inform, persuade) honest about what you're doing?

stages.label: Researching
questions: Who created your strongest source, and why did they create it?
Have you gone upstream to the original study, document, or data?
What do other sources say about your most important source?
Which main point has the least support right now?

stages.label: Organizing
questions: Why does your first main point come first?
Could a listener predict your next point from your transitions?
Which pattern did you choose, and what would change with a different one?
Does every main point support your central idea?

stages.label: Rehearsing
questions: Where did you stumble in your last practice run, and why?
Which sentence matters most, and how will you deliver it?
Where will you pause?
What will you do if you lose your place?

stages.label: Reflecting
questions: What did your audience respond to most?
What evidence do you have for that (not just a feeling)?
What is one specific thing you will do differently next time?
How does this speech compare to your first one?

prompts.title: Topic brainstorm partner
prompts.text: Act as a speech coach, not a writer. I'm a [high school / college] student preparing a [speech type]. My interests are: [list]. Ask me five questions, one at a time, that help me find a focused topic. Do not suggest a finished topic or write any part of my speech.

prompts.title: Purpose and thesis check
prompts.text: Act as a speech coach. Here is my specific purpose and central idea: [paste]. Using these guidelines (one idea, infinitive phrase for purpose, complete declarative sentence for central idea, verb matches content), tell me which guideline each statement meets or misses. Ask me a question to help me revise. Do not rewrite them for me.

prompts.title: Skeptical audience practice
prompts.text: Play a fair but skeptical audience member. My persuasive claim is: [claim]. My main reasons are: [reasons]. Ask me one tough question at a time and wait for my answer. After each answer, tell me whether I used evidence or only opinion.

prompts.title: Outline gap finder
prompts.text: Act as a speech coach. Here is my outline: [paste]. Identify which main points lack evidence, where transitions are missing, and whether each point supports my central idea. Do not add content or examples. Ask me questions instead.

prompts.title: Concept explainer
prompts.text: Explain [concept, e.g. Monroe's Motivated Sequence] to a [high school / college] student in plain language with one original example that is NOT about my topic. Then ask me to explain it back in my own words and tell me what I got right or missed.
